screens.title: Challenges of Petabyte-Scale Migration
screens.narratorSegment: Large-data migration introduces constraints you rarely face with smaller moves. Bandwidth becomes a primary limiter: a modest upload pipe can stretch a migration over weeks or months, increasing costs and operational risk. Security and compliance add operational steps: encryption at rest and in transit, IAM restriction, and audit logging all slow and complicate execution. Data integrity matters more: errors that are rare at file-by-file scale can become costly when millions of files are in play, so systematic checksum validation is required. Cost is another dimension—network egress fees, per-job device charges, and staff time add up. A common misconception is that a long-running network transfer is always cheaper than physical shipment. In many cases the hourly cost of bandwidth, the risk of re-transmission for errors, and the time value of data make offline physical devices like Snowball Edge or Snowmobile more economical. A good approach is to quantify throughput limits, run a pilot transfer for a representative dataset, and then select a transfer pattern. For example, measure effective throughput on a 1 Gbps link during business hours and during off-peak windows, and use those figures to estimate time and cost. The key takeaway is that scale changes priorities: plan around bandwidth, integrity, security, and cost rather than only tooling comfort.

screens.title: AWS DataSync: Online Transfer and Synchronization
screens.narratorSegment: AWS DataSync simplifies and accelerates networked transfers between on-premises storage and AWS targets like S3, EFS, and FSx. At a high level, you deploy a DataSync agent on-premises to connect to NFS, SMB, or object storage. The agent talks to DataSync over TLS, and DataSync then manages parallel data streams, retries, and integrity verification. This makes it significantly faster than basic copy tools in many cases. A concrete example is syncing an on-premises NFS share of 10 terabytes to S3 on a 1 Gbps Direct Connect link; DataSync uses concurrent streams and efficient protocols to maximize throughput while handling encryption and checksums automatically. A common misconception is that DataSync simply wraps rsync; instead, it employs a purpose-built protocol and managed task options like point-in-time consistency and overwrite policies. When designing a DataSync migration, include agent placement, network path testing, IAM roles for S3 access, and a CloudWatch log group for task monitoring. Start with a small task, verify integrity, then scale the task schedule. The takeaway is that DataSync is the right choice for ongoing synchronization and accelerated online transfers where network connectivity is reliable and security requirements are met.

Process Flow

Agent → DataSync → S3/EFS

Deploy an agent on-prem, configure source and destination locations, create a task, and run scheduled or ad-hoc transfers.

Agent deployment
Deploy a VM image and activate the agent with a key to connect on-prem storage to DataSync.
Task configuration
Set verify mode, overwrite behavior, and logging to CloudWatch to meet integrity and audit requirements.
Performance
DataSync uses parallel streams and an optimized protocol to outperform general-purpose copy tools.
Key Takeaway

DataSync is optimized for secure, accelerated online transfers and ongoing synchronization; include agent placement, IAM, and monitoring in your plan.

Concrete example & code
A conceptual set of CLI steps shows how a DataSync task is created and started. Use the AWS CLI to create agent, locations, task, then start the task. The service handles integrity checks and parallelization.
# --- AWS CLI commands for DataSync (conceptual) ---

# 1. Create a DataSync Agent (on-premises)
# aws datasync create-agent --agent-name "OnPremAgent01" --activation-key "your-activation-key"

# 2. Create a source location (NFS)
aws datasync create-location-nfs \
    --server-hostname "your-nfs-server.local" \
    --subdirectory "/export/data" \
    --on-prem-config "AgentArns=arn:aws:datasync:us-east-1:123456789012:agent/agent-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx" \
    --tags Key=Name,Value=OnPremNFSLocation

# 3. Create a target location (S3)
aws datasync create-location-s3 \
    --s3-bucket-arn "arn:aws:s3:::your-target-bucket" \
    --s3-config "BucketAccessRoleArn=arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/DataSyncS3AccessRole" \
    --tags Key=Name,Value=TargetS3Location

# 4. Create and start a DataSync task
aws datasync create-task \
    --source-location-arn "arn:aws:datasync:us-east-1:123456789012:location/loc-xxxxxxxx" \
    --destination-location-arn "arn:aws:datasync:us-east-1:123456789012:location/loc-yyyyyyyy" \
    --cloud-watch-log-group-arn "arn:aws:logs:us-east-1:123456789012:log-group:/aws/datasync/task/your-task-name" \
    --name "MigrateNFSDataToS3" \
    --options VerifyMode=POINT_IN_TIME_CONSISTENT,OverwriteMode=ALWAYS,TaskQueueing=ENABLED

# Start:
# aws datasync start-task-execution --task-arn "arn:aws:datasync:us-east-1:..."
Misconception
Don't assume DataSync is a drop-in for legacy FTP workflows; it's built for system-to-system transfers and synchronization. For protocol compatibility with partners, consider Transfer Family instead.

screens.title: AWS Transfer Family and Legacy File Workflows
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Transfer Family lets organizations continue using standard file-transfer protocols while moving files directly into Amazon S3 or Amazon EFS. This is particularly useful when external partners or legacy systems expect SFTP, FTPS, or FTP endpoints. Instead of reengineering client software, you create a managed endpoint and map incoming files into buckets or file systems. As an example, organizations that receive daily uploads from partners over SFTP can migrate to Transfer Family to eliminate in-house FTP servers while preserving the client experience. A frequent misconception is that Transfer Family is intended for bulk archival migration; it is optimized for protocol compatibility and ongoing partner workflows. For large bulk loads, DataSync or Snow Family are often better fits. When designing with Transfer Family, include authentication options, logging for auditing, and IAM roles to restrict access to target storage. Also evaluate network placement—keeping traffic inside AWS with VPC endpoints can improve security and sometimes cost. The key takeaway is that Transfer Family preserves client workflows and provides a managed path into AWS storage without requiring client-side changes. Definition

Protocol-compatible file transfer

Offer SFTP, FTPS, or FTP endpoints that deposit files into S3 or EFS without changing external clients.

Concrete scenario
A partner with existing SFTP clients continues to upload daily files. You replace the on-prem server with Transfer Family, preserving client behavior while storing files directly in S3 for analytics.
Design items
  • Authentication method and user mapping.
  • IAM role mapping to target buckets or file systems.
  • CloudWatch logging for auditing transfers.
When to choose Transfer Family
  • External partners require unchanged client behavior.
  • Daily to frequent transfers of small-to-medium size files.

screens.title: AWS Snow Family Overview
screens.narratorSegment: The AWS Snow Family provides physical devices for offline data transfer and edge compute. Snowcone is the smallest device, rugged and secure, suitable for harsh environments and smaller migrations up to about 8 terabytes usable. Snowball Edge offers larger capacities and optional compute; storage-optimized variants provide up to roughly 80 terabytes usable and are useful when you need to transfer big datasets or run temporary edge processing. At the extreme end, Snowmobile is a 45-foot shipping container capable of moving tens to hundreds of petabytes—AWS describes it as used for exabyte-scale transfers in constrained network environments. You use Snow Family when network bandwidth is insufficient or prohibitively expensive for the timeframe required. The devices are physically shipped, connected to local networks for data copy, then returned to AWS for secure ingestion into S3. Security features include 256-bit encryption, tamper-evident enclosures, and strict chain-of-custody procedures. A common misconception is that physical devices are lower security; in fact, Snow devices are designed with strong physical and cryptographic protections. The main trade-offs are logistics and per-job fees versus ongoing network costs and time.

Snowcone
Small, rugged device for edge and smaller migrations (up to about 8 TB usable). Useful where space is limited or environments are harsh.
Snowball Edge
Larger capacity and optional compute. Storage-optimized appliances can hold around 80 TB usable and support temporary edge processing while migrating data.
Snowmobile
A 45-foot shipping container for exabyte-scale transfers, designed for moving tens to hundreds of petabytes when networks are impractical.
Security & process
Devices are encrypted before they leave your site, use tamper-evident enclosures, and are tracked through chain-of-custody processes. The workflow is: order device, connect locally, copy data, ship back to AWS, and have data ingested into S3.

screens.title: Snow Family Operational Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Using the Snow Family follows a consistent operational flow. First, you order the device and AWS ships it to your site. Next, you connect the device to your local network and copy data to the device using the provided tools. During copy, data is encrypted locally using device-provided keys; access to the device requires an unlock process that uses service-generated credentials. Once the device is filled or the job completes, you ship it back to AWS, where the device is ingested and the data uploaded to your S3 bucket. Security controls include tamper-evident packaging, 256-bit encryption, and chain-of-custody tracking so you can meet compliance requirements. A common misconception is that physical shipment eliminates the need for careful planning; in reality, logistics, physical access, and customs can introduce delays and constraints. For large jobs, plan buffer time for shipping, customs, and ingestion, and consider parallelizing across multiple devices when you have many hundreds of terabytes. The practical takeaway is to treat Snow migrations like projects with logistics, security checkpoints, and testing; run a test load and validate checksums before full-scale execution.

Process Flow
  1. Order device — Plan capacity and timeline, order appropriate Snow device.
  2. Connect & copy — Attach device to local network and use provided tools to copy data, ensuring encryption is enabled.
  3. Ship to AWS — Return the device with chain-of-custody tracking enabled.

  • Consider parallel devices to shorten overall migration time.

For a 500 TB archive with limited bandwidth, order multiple Snowball Edge devices, copy partitions of the archive in parallel, and ship them back staggered to reduce overall migration time.
Common mistake

Underestimating logistics and not allowing buffer time for shipping, customs, and ingestion leads to missed deadlines even when physical transfer is chosen.

screens.title: Online vs Offline Transfer Comparison
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between online and offline transfer approaches requires comparing volume, bandwidth, urgency, and cost. Online options—DataSync and Transfer Family—work well when you have reliable network connectivity and the dataset fits a schedule that tolerates the transfer time. DataSync is ideal for system-to-system synchronization and bulk online transfers, while Transfer Family preserves protocol compatibility for partner workflows. screens.title: Performance and Cost Optimization
screens.narratorSegment: Optimizing performance and cost requires combining network engineering and transfer strategy. Parallelization increases throughput: use tools and services that support multiple concurrent streams to saturate available bandwidth without exceeding network policies. DataSync inherently parallelizes and manages retries, making it a strong choice for maximizing throughput. Direct Connect provides a dedicated network path with consistent throughput and often lower per-GB costs than public internet egress; use it when you expect large, frequent transfers. Compression and deduplication reduce bytes moved, saving cost and time; pre-process archives where possible. Scheduling transfers during off-peak windows reduces contention with other traffic and improves effective throughput. Cost considerations mean comparing DataSync per-GB charges, Snow Family per-job fees and daily charges, and Transfer Family per-endpoint/per-GB pricing. Always compute the total landed cost: device fees, shipping, ingestion time, plus any network egress or service fees. A typical misconception is that adding more parallel streams always helps; without measurement, more streams can congest the network and reduce overall efficiency. Run experiments that vary stream counts and measure achieved throughput, then choose the concurrency level that reliably uses available bandwidth without creating packet loss or re-transmits.

screens.title: Data Integrity: Checksums and Verification
screens.narratorSegment: Data integrity is non-negotiable when moving large datasets. Checksums are compact digital fingerprints used to verify that source and destination data match. The recommended practice is to compute and record checksums before transfer, let the transfer service perform its own integrity checks, and then validate checksums after ingestion. DataSync automates integrity validation during transfer, but you should still independently verify important archives. For Snow devices, compute local checksums and compare them after AWS ingests the data into S3. A typical mistake is relying solely on successful transfer job status without performing independent checksum comparisons; job success does not guarantee content-level integrity in every failure scenario. A concrete example: for a 10 TB archive, produce SHA-256 checksums for archives or file batches, store them in a manifest, and verify after the transfer completes. If mismatches occur, isolate and retransmit only the affected parts. The practical takeaway is to bake checksum generation and verification into your migration plan and automate the comparison to scale verification across millions of files. Large-scale data migration requires more than copying files. When you move hundreds of terabytes or petabytes, network limits, costs, and compliance rules shape which approach will work. In this lesson we’ll situate the major AWS options—DataSync for accelerated network transfers, Transfer Family for protocol-compatible file exchange, and the Snow Family for offline physical movement—and explain when each is the most practical choice. You will learn criteria to evaluate: data volume, available bandwidth, urgency, security and chain-of-custody needs, and cost trade-offs. We’ll also walk through concrete examples, including a simulated DataSync task and migration scenarios that map directly to Snowcone, Snowball Edge, and Snowmobile. By the end you should be able to decide when to use an online transfer, when to ship physical devices, and how to optimize throughput and integrity. Think of this chapter as a decision toolkit: know the services, validate with a small pilot, and choose the option that balances schedule, cost, and compliance. Which constraint matters most for your migration?

These objectives map to practical skills you need for large-scale migration. First, you will evaluate AWS data transfer services by matching data volume, bandwidth, and security requirements to each service. That means practicing trade-off analysis and choosing a service based on constraints, not preference. Second, you will design solutions for petabyte-scale moves using the AWS Snow Family, understanding device capacities, physical workflow, and chain-of-custody. Third, you will implement hybrid synchronization patterns using AWS DataSync and Transfer Family so on-premises systems remain consistent with cloud buckets. Fourth, you will optimize transfer performance and costs by applying techniques like parallelization, scheduling, and using Direct Connect where appropriate. Each objective includes a competency milestone you can verify by running a pilot migration, validating checksums, and documenting an approval-ready migration plan. Large-data migration introduces constraints you rarely face with smaller moves. Bandwidth becomes a primary limiter: a modest upload pipe can stretch a migration over weeks or months, increasing costs and operational risk. Security and compliance add operational steps: encryption at rest and in transit, IAM restriction, and audit logging all slow and complicate execution. Data integrity matters more: errors that are rare at file-by-file scale can become costly when millions of files are in play, so systematic checksum validation is required. Cost is another dimension—network egress fees, per-job device charges, and staff time add up. A common misconception is that a long-running network transfer is always cheaper than physical shipment. In many cases the hourly cost of bandwidth, the risk of re-transmission for errors, and the time value of data make offline physical devices like Snowball Edge or Snowmobile more economical. A good approach is to quantify throughput limits, run a pilot transfer for a representative dataset, and then select a transfer pattern. For example, measure effective throughput on a 1 Gbps link during business hours and during off-peak windows, and use those figures to estimate time and cost. The key takeaway is that scale changes priorities: plan around bandwidth, integrity, security, and cost rather than only tooling comfort.

AWS DataSync simplifies and accelerates networked transfers between on-premises storage and AWS targets like S3, EFS, and FSx. At a high level, you deploy a DataSync agent on-premises to connect to NFS, SMB, or object storage. The agent talks to DataSync over TLS, and DataSync then manages parallel data streams, retries, and integrity verification. This makes it significantly faster than basic copy tools in many cases. A concrete example is syncing an on-premises NFS share of 10 terabytes to S3 on a 1 Gbps Direct Connect link; DataSync uses concurrent streams and efficient protocols to maximize throughput while handling encryption and checksums automatically. A common misconception is that DataSync simply wraps rsync; instead, it employs a purpose-built protocol and managed task options like point-in-time consistency and overwrite policies. When designing a DataSync migration, include agent placement, network path testing, IAM roles for S3 access, and a CloudWatch log group for task monitoring. Start with a small task, verify integrity, then scale the task schedule. The takeaway is that DataSync is the right choice for ongoing synchronization and accelerated online transfers where network connectivity is reliable and security requirements are met.

AWS Transfer Family lets organizations continue using standard file-transfer protocols while moving files directly into Amazon S3 or Amazon EFS. This is particularly useful when external partners or legacy systems expect SFTP, FTPS, or FTP endpoints. Instead of reengineering client software, you create a managed endpoint and map incoming files into buckets or file systems. As an example, organizations that receive daily uploads from partners over SFTP can migrate to Transfer Family to eliminate in-house FTP servers while preserving the client experience. A frequent misconception is that Transfer Family is intended for bulk archival migration; it is optimized for protocol compatibility and ongoing partner workflows. For large bulk loads, DataSync or Snow Family are often better fits. When designing with Transfer Family, include authentication options, logging for auditing, and IAM roles to restrict access to target storage. Also evaluate network placement—keeping traffic inside AWS with VPC endpoints can improve security and sometimes cost. The key takeaway is that Transfer Family preserves client workflows and provides a managed path into AWS storage without requiring client-side changes. The AWS Snow Family provides physical devices for offline data transfer and edge compute. Snowcone is the smallest device, rugged and secure, suitable for harsh environments and smaller migrations up to about 8 terabytes usable. Snowball Edge offers larger capacities and optional compute; storage-optimized variants provide up to roughly 80 terabytes usable and are useful when you need to transfer big datasets or run temporary edge processing. At the extreme end, Snowmobile is a 45-foot shipping container capable of moving tens to hundreds of petabytes—AWS describes it as used for exabyte-scale transfers in constrained network environments. You use Snow Family when network bandwidth is insufficient or prohibitively expensive for the timeframe required. The devices are physically shipped, connected to local networks for data copy, then returned to AWS for secure ingestion into S3. Security features include 256-bit encryption, tamper-evident enclosures, and strict chain-of-custody procedures. A common misconception is that physical devices are lower security; in fact, Snow devices are designed with strong physical and cryptographic protections. The main trade-offs are logistics and per-job fees versus ongoing network costs and time.

Using the Snow Family follows a consistent operational flow. First, you order the device and AWS ships it to your site. Next, you connect the device to your local network and copy data to the device using the provided tools. During copy, data is encrypted locally using device-provided keys; access to the device requires an unlock process that uses service-generated credentials. Once the device is filled or the job completes, you ship it back to AWS, where the device is ingested and the data uploaded to your S3 bucket. Security controls include tamper-evident packaging, 256-bit encryption, and chain-of-custody tracking so you can meet compliance requirements. A common misconception is that physical shipment eliminates the need for careful planning; in reality, logistics, physical access, and customs can introduce delays and constraints. For large jobs, plan buffer time for shipping, customs, and ingestion, and consider parallelizing across multiple devices when you have many hundreds of terabytes. The practical takeaway is to treat Snow migrations like projects with logistics, security checkpoints, and testing; run a test load and validate checksums before full-scale execution.

Choosing between online and offline transfer approaches requires comparing volume, bandwidth, urgency, and cost. Online options—DataSync and Transfer Family—work well when you have reliable network connectivity and the dataset fits a schedule that tolerates the transfer time. DataSync is ideal for system-to-system synchronization and bulk online transfers, while Transfer Family preserves protocol compatibility for partner workflows. Offline options, the Snow Family, are chosen when network bandwidth is insufficient, when cost of long-term transfer is higher than device shipment, or when regulatory or logistical needs demand physical transport. For instance, if you must move 80 PB in six months with no feasible network path, Snowmobile is appropriate; conversely, a continuous 10 TB sync between an on-prem NFS and S3 over Direct Connect is suited to DataSync. Misconceptions include believing offline is always slower or more risky; Snow devices are purpose-built with strong encryption and chain-of-custody processes. The pragmatic strategy is to quantify effective throughput, estimate costs for both approaches, and pilot a representative subset. Then select the approach that satisfies timeline, budget, and compliance requirements. Optimizing performance and cost requires combining network engineering and transfer strategy. Parallelization increases throughput: use tools and services that support multiple concurrent streams to saturate available bandwidth without exceeding network policies. DataSync inherently parallelizes and manages retries, making it a strong choice for maximizing throughput. Direct Connect provides a dedicated network path with consistent throughput and often lower per-GB costs than public internet egress; use it when you expect large, frequent transfers. Compression and deduplication reduce bytes moved, saving cost and time; pre-process archives where possible. Scheduling transfers during off-peak windows reduces contention with other traffic and improves effective throughput. Cost considerations mean comparing DataSync per-GB charges, Snow Family per-job fees and daily charges, and Transfer Family per-endpoint/per-GB pricing. Always compute the total landed cost: device fees, shipping, ingestion time, plus any network egress or service fees. A typical misconception is that adding more parallel streams always helps; without measurement, more streams can congest the network and reduce overall efficiency. Run experiments that vary stream counts and measure achieved throughput, then choose the concurrency level that reliably uses available bandwidth without creating packet loss or re-transmits.

Security and compliance practices must be integral to any large-data migration. Encrypt data in transit and at rest: DataSync uses TLS for transfers and Snow devices encrypt stored data with strong cryptography before they leave your site. Implement strict IAM policies so only designated roles and services can access migration tasks and target buckets. Use VPC endpoints where possible to keep traffic inside the AWS network and reduce exposure to the internet. Enable CloudTrail to capture A P I activity for auditing: logs show who created agents, started tasks, or issued device unlocks, which is essential for compliance. For Snow Family, maintain a documented chain-of-custody and control who holds the device unlock credentials. A common misconception is that physically shipping a device removes audit requirements—on the contrary, it needs stronger documentation of custody and access. Also ensure that compliance frameworks you must follow—such as regional data residency rules—are considered before shipping devices across borders. The practical takeaway is to bake-in encryption, RBAC, VPC isolation, and audit logging early in the migration plan and validate them during the pilot. Data integrity is non-negotiable when moving large datasets. Checksums are compact digital fingerprints used to verify that source and destination data match. The recommended practice is to compute and record checksums before transfer, let the transfer service perform its own integrity checks, and then validate checksums after ingestion. DataSync automates integrity validation during transfer, but you should still independently verify important archives. For Snow devices, compute local checksums and compare them after AWS ingests the data into S3. A typical mistake is relying solely on successful transfer job status without performing independent checksum comparisons; job success does not guarantee content-level integrity in every failure scenario. A concrete example: for a 10 TB archive, produce SHA-256 checksums for archives or file batches, store them in a manifest, and verify after the transfer completes. If mismatches occur, isolate and retransmit only the affected parts. The practical takeaway is to bake checksum generation and verification into your migration plan and automate the comparison to scale verification across millions of files. Teams frequently underestimate transfer time and the operational overhead of large migrations. Two common mistakes are relying on theoretical bandwidth instead of measured effective throughput, and skipping a pilot migration. Effective throughput is often lower than link capacity due to congestion, protocol overhead, and competing traffic. A pilot validates real-world throughput, reveals bottlenecks like misconfigured network stacks or firewall rules, and tests integrity procedures. Another common error is choosing the wrong tool—using rsync or ad-hoc copies instead of DataSync or Snow devices for large bulk transfers leads to poor performance and management headaches. To run a meaningful pilot, select a representative subset of data, measure end-to-end time, validate checksum workflows, and test security settings and audit logs. Document the outcomes and update cost and time estimates. Treat the pilot as a short project with acceptance criteria: throughput meets minimums, checksums validate, and monitoring and IAM policies function as expected. The takeaway is to invest time in a small pilot: it uncovers costly surprises and ensures the full migration runs predictably.
